title: Kimchi Probiotic May Help Flush Nanoplastics From the Body
summary:
The World Institute of Kimchi, a government-funded research institute in South Korea, announced that a lactic acid bacterium isolated from kimchi can help remove nanoplastics from the body by binding to them in the intestine.

Nanoplastics are ultrafine plastic particles measuring less than 1 micrometer—one-thousandth of a millimeter. They form when larger plastics break down and can enter the body through food and drinking water. Because they are so small, nanoplastics may cross the intestinal barrier and accumulate in organs such as the kidneys and brain. Biological strategies to reduce this accumulation remain at an early stage of research.

A team led by Drs. Se Hee Lee and Tae Woong Whon at WiKim tested a kimchi-derived lactic acid bacterium, Leuconostoc mesenteroides CBA3656, against polystyrene nanoplastics. Under standard lab conditions, strain CBA3656 showed 87% adsorption efficiency, comparable to reference strain Latilactobacillus sakei CBA3608 at 85%. But under simulated human intestinal conditions, strain CBA3608 dropped sharply to 3%, while CBA3656 maintained 57%. This suggests the kimchi strain can stably bind nanoplastics in environments resembling the human intestinal tract.

In animal experiments using germ-free mice, both male and female mice given strain CBA3656 showed more than a twofold increase in nanoplastics detected in feces compared with a control group that received no probiotics. This suggests the probiotic may help excrete nanoplastics by binding to them in the intestine.

The study provides scientific evidence that kimchi-derived lactic acid bacteria may interact with environmental micropollutants beyond their traditional role in fermentation, offering new insight into biological mechanisms that may help reduce nanoplastic accumulation in the gastrointestinal tract.

"Plastic pollution is increasingly recognized not only as an environmental issue but also as a public health concern," said Dr. Sehee Lee, the lead researcher. "Our findings suggest that microorganisms derived from traditional fermented foods could represent a new biological approach to address this emerging challenge. We will continue to expand the scientific value of kimchi microbial resources to contribute to public health and environmental solutions."

The study was supported by the National Research Council of Science & Technology. While promising, more research is needed to see if the same effect occurs in humans. If it does, kimchi bacteria could become a new tool to fight plastic pollution inside our bodies.
why_it_matters: Plastic pollution is now a health question as well as an environmental one, and this study suggests part of the answer might come from unexpected places — traditional fermented foods and their microbes. It also shows why a promising lab result is not a solution: turning a mouse and test-tube finding into human advice takes years of further research, and it does not replace cutting plastic waste at the source.

background_read: Kimchi is a traditional Korean dish of salted, fermented vegetables, and the lactic acid bacteria that ferment it belong to the same broad family of microbes that turn milk into yogurt and cabbage into sauerkraut. The study came from the World Institute of Kimchi (WiKim), a government-funded research centre in South Korea devoted to studying the food and its microbes, with support from the National Research Council of Science & Technology (a South Korean government body that funds research institutes).

Nanoplastics are plastic fragments smaller than one micrometer — far thinner than a human hair — that break off bags, bottles and clothing and end up in water and food. In recent years scientists have reported finding microplastic and nanoplastic particles in human blood, lungs and other tissue, although the health effects are still uncertain and debated.

Researchers use germ-free mice — animals raised with no microbes of their own — so they can add a single bacterial strain and see exactly what it does. The kimchi strain tested here, Leuconostoc mesenteroides CBA3656, belongs to a group already widely used in food fermentation, which is one reason scientists hope it could eventually be tested safely in people. The big caveat: a test-tube and mouse result is not proof of a human benefit.

perspectives.description: A bacterium taken from a food eaten for centuries could become a low-cost biological tool against plastic accumulation, and it held up far better than a reference strain under gut-like conditions. The work also expands the scientific value of kimchi's microbial resources beyond fermentation.

The headline numbers come from lab assays and germ-free mice, not people; the human gut is far more complex and may behave differently. Binding plastic in the intestine does not automatically mean less plastic reaching organs, and claims about a 'probiotic fix' could distract from reducing plastic production and waste.

This fits a wider research trend of studying how diet and gut microbes interact with pollutants, with fermented foods long serving as a source of candidate probiotic strains. The comparison of performance under standard versus simulated intestinal conditions is what makes the result interesting rather than the raw percentages alone.

The obvious next step is human trials, followed by tests against other kinds of plastic beyond polystyrene. Scientists would also need to track whether binding actually lowers long-term accumulation in organs such as the kidneys and brain — the effect that would matter most for health.
